title: England hasn't found the Holy Grail...but...
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Writing five weeks after moving to Australia, Haili Hughes reflects on what England's decade-long adoption of the science of learning has actually achieved for the teaching profession. She recalls how disruptive the shift was for practitioners like herself, arguing that it unsettled professional identity and turned research into something teachers themselves could own. Her central claim is that England has built a shared mental model of how learning happens, embedded in ITT, the Early Career Framework, the Core Content Framework and NPQs, so that new teachers are now trained on it and carry it into middle leadership. She identifies the EEF's 2021 mechanisms of PD report as the pivotal change that shifted professional development from one-off inspirational keynotes to structured, sustained expertise-building. Looking ahead, she argues that the next phase is valuing evidence without losing professional judgement, warning Australia against the top-down non-negotiable lesson frameworks many English schools first adopted. She concludes that England has not found the Holy Grail but has uncovered valuable clues.
points: Hughes argues that the science of learning has moved from small pockets of enthusiasts to the shared language of English teaching, citing visits to around 150 schools a year where every staff had at least heard the terms.

The 'Golden Thread' of ITT reaccreditation, the ECF, CCF and NPQs is credited with making evidence-informed training universal for new teachers, producing a trickle-down effect as they reach middle leadership.
She singles out the EEF's 2021 mechanisms of PD report as a game changer that ended one-and-done keynotes and prompted scrutiny of the credibility of those delivering PD.

Evidence-informed practice is framed not as telling teachers exactly what to do but as giving them better tools for professional decisions, a lesson she urges Australia to learn before copying rigid top-down lesson frameworks.
quotes: One thing I have really missed is the coherent, shared mental model that much of the system in England seems to hold about how learning happens. This was not an easy-won fight. By the time I had heard about the science of learning, I had been teaching for over a decade.

This was a profession that was beginning to change and with change, comes all sorts of feelings. Excitement and hope at new possibilities. Yet, also anxiety and fear - a loss of confidence and professional identity.

But it also disrupted the old established orders. Research was no longer something that academics owned and disseminated to teachers. Teachers were now making their own professional decisions about what research meant to their practice.

This means that all new teachers in England, are trained using a framework for their first 3 years which is built on the foundations of how students learn. These new teachers are moving towards middle leadership, so we get the trickle-down effect.

Perhaps the biggest shift I have noticed is how teachers and leaders talk about expertise. It isn’t about getting better at teaching through vibes and osmosis, or teaching being an art that you are just born with. It is the growing realisation that teachers get better through structured support and continual refinement.

For years, I sat through one and done, ‘inspirational’ key notes which made absolutely no impact on my skills as a practitioner. For the first time, these mechanisms told those delivering PD what mechanisms they should include to really help teachers make the most of the time they had with teachers.
It gives teachers better tools for making professional decisions. Loads of schools and MATs went really top down with non-negotiable lesson frameworks etc, which is what I see happening here.
